Article Title: Meta's highest-paid employee Alexandr Wang can't stop making fun of Google, says who is ...
Article Text:
Meta AI head

The benchmark behind Alexandr Wang’s dig at Google

Where the gains came from

The cost advantage

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and highest-paid employee recently took a jab at Google ’s Gemini after a benchmark data shoed Meta’s latest AU model climbing near the very top of the industry rankings. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Wang wrote, “I really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 🚀💨” alongside a performance chart showing Meta’s Muse Spark 1.3 surpassing several Gemini variants on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. According to Artificial Analysis, Muse Spark 1.3 scored 62 points, placing it behind only Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 (66) and Claude Opus 5 (63). The model outperformed Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro and Gemini 1.5 Flash, which scored 61 and 53 respectively.Wang's comment was posted in response to a thread from Artificial Analysis announcing that Meta had released Muse Spark 1.3, the company's fourth Muse Spark model release in just five months. According to the benchmark firm, Muse Spark 1.3 (max) — currently in limited preview for Meta's partners — scored 62 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, trailing only Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 in their top configurations.The publicly available variant, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh), scored 61 on the same index, putting it in a tie with GPT-5.6 Sol (max), Grok 4.6 (high), and Claude Opus 5 (high). That score represents a 4-point jump from Muse Spark 1.2's score of 57 in August, and an 8-point gain over Muse Spark 1.1's score of 53 in July. It landed just behind Claude Fable 5.1 (max, 66), Claude Opus 5 (max, 63), and Claude Fable 5 (max, 62).According to Artificial Analysis, both new Muse Spark variants improved primarily in two areas: agentic task performance and scientific reasoning.On agentic work, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh) posted a 12-point gain over Muse Spark 1.2 on the Tau3-Bench Banking evaluation, rising from 35% to 47%, along with a 5-point gain on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (80% to 85%) and a jump in GDPval-AA v2 Elo rating from 1,615 to 1,709. The limited-preview Muse Spark 1.3 (max) variant pushed even further, reaching 52% on Tau3-Bench Banking — the highest score of any model on that specific benchmark — and a GDPval-AA v2 Elo of 1,754. Artificial Analysis noted that Muse Spark 1.3 (max) achieves these higher scores in part by using significantly more reasoning tokens than the xhigh variant, reasoning 62% more on GDPval-AA v2 and 28% more on Tau3-Bench Banking.On scientific reasoning, the standout gain came on CritPt, where the xhigh variant improved 8 points over Muse Spark 1.2, from 18% to 26%. GPQA Diamond rose 4 points, from 90% to 94%, while Humanity's Last Exam and SciCode each posted more modest 2-to-3-point gains.Beyond performance, Muse Spark 1.3 also demonstrated efficiency. The xhigh variant costs about $0.55 per task, significantly lower than GPT‑5.6 Sol and Grok 4.6, which cost nearly double. Analysts noted this places Muse Spark on the “Pareto frontier” for intelligence versus cost, making it one of the most competitive models in terms of value.For those unaware, Meta has released four Muse Spark models in just five months, underscoring its aggressive push in frontier AI.

Wang wrote, “I really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 🚀💨” alongside a performance chart showing Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 surpassing several Gemini variants on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. According to the benchmark firm, Muse Spark1.3 (max) — currently in limited preview for Meta's partners — scored 62.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity; decades later scientists found the plantations were changing groundwater but not the soil nature
Article Text:
Eucalyptus cladocalyx ‘nana’. Image Credit: ERA Nurseries

How did eucalyptus plantations change groundwater and soil salinity in Australia

The groundwater changed, but the saline seep remained

Why didn't the eucalyptus trees solve the salinity problem

Image Credit: AI generated

Some eucalyptus species performed better over 15 years

nana

A long-term lesson from Australia's eucalyptus plantations

Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity, hoping that thirsty, deep-rooted vegetation could help control the groundwater processes behind the problem. A long-running experiment in south-western Australia later showed that the effects of such plantations were more complicated than simply planting trees and waiting for the land to recover. Researchers established a mixed eucalyptus plantation above a saline seep in 1976 and monitored how the trees affected groundwater levels and salt movement for 15 years. The study found clear signs that the plantation used more water than nearby crops and pasture, while groundwater conditions also changed over time. Yet the trees did not stop the saline seep as researchers had hoped. Published in ‘ Agricultural Water Management ,’ this comprehensive study reveals that effective land management requires understanding complex underground hydrological systems, cautioning against oversimplified solutions to persistent environmental challenges like soil salinity.The study examined a plantation established on about 12% of a small farm catchment. The trees were planted above a saline seep, an area where salty groundwater had reached or approached the surface and damaged the land. The researchers wanted to identify eucalyptus species that could use large amounts of water and potentially help reclaim such affected areas. According to the study, the catchment contained two important groundwater systems.One was a deep aquifer in the lower part of the landscape and the other, a shallower seasonal aquifer. The researchers monitored changes in groundwater level and salinity using piezometers, allowing them to follow how conditions changed as the plantation developed.The results showed that the plantation was having a noticeable effect on water use. Changes in groundwater levels, along with observations of perched water, indicated that the trees were using more water than the nearby crop and pasture vegetation. This was an important finding because the basic idea behind planting trees in salt-affected agricultural landscapes was that trees could alter the movement of water through the soil. If less water moved downwards into the groundwater system, or if trees removed more water from the landscape, they could potentially help limit the processes that bring salt towards the surface.The researchers found that the plantation influenced groundwater chemistry as well as water levels. Chloride concentrations in the deep aquifer fell by approximately 20% between 1977 and 1984. The decline was greater at the middle of the slope than further downslope. This suggested that conditions beneath the catchment were changing, although the changes were not uniform across the landscape. At the same time, the study found larger stores of salt in the soil downslope than at the middle of the slope. There was also visual evidence that salt continued to be discharged extensively through the saline seep throughout the experiment. In other words, the trees were clearly affecting the local water system, but their presence did not bring the expected recovery of the seep. The research showed why this distinction matters. A plantation may increase water use and change groundwater conditions without having enough influence over the particular underground system responsible for a saline area. The findings also suggested that surface changes alone could not explain what was happening beneath the catchment, where groundwater pathways controlled the movement of salt.One of the most important findings of the study concerned the location of the plantation. The researchers identified the site's underground geology as a significant reason why the trees failed to control the seepage. The plantation was located in an area where the relevant aquifer appeared to be ‘confined.’ That meant the groundwater system beneath the site was not easy for the trees to influence in the way researchers had hoped. This finding highlighted a practical limitation of tree-based approaches to salinity. Planting species that use substantial amounts of water may not be enough on its own. The location of groundwater, the way water moves through underground layers and the position of the plantation within the wider landscape can all affect the outcome. The study therefore showed that managing salinity is not simply a question of selecting the thirstiest trees. Understanding the underground environment is equally important.The experiment also compared the performance of different eucalyptus species. The original aim was to rank species partly according to water use, which the researchers assessed through factors including leaf area and survival. Tree growth was rapid during the early years of the experiment, continuing strongly until 1981. After that, growth declined. 15 years later, four species emerged as the most promising among those tested. These included ‘Eucalyptus cladocalyx var.,’ ‘Eucalyptus cladocalyx,’ ‘Eucalyptus occidentalis’ and ‘Eucalyptus sargentii.’ Their performance did not mean that the plantation had solved the saline seep problem. Instead, it showed that some species were better suited than others to the demanding conditions of the site. A tree can survive well and use considerable amounts of water while still being unable to alter a groundwater system enough to stop salt from reaching the surface.The 15-year experiment provided a more realistic picture of what tree planting could not achieve in salt-affected farmland. The eucalyptus plantation used more water than the surrounding vegetation, and conditions in the deep groundwater system also shifted, including a significant fall in chloride concentration. Yet the saline seep continued to discharge salt. As per the study, this outcome was due to the underground conditions beneath the plantation. The research pointed towards a broader lesson that the success of planting trees depends not only on the trees, but also on the landscape in which they are planted. For areas struggling with rising groundwater and soil salinity, the findings suggest that planting eucalyptus can be a useful tool, but it is not a solution. Trees can change groundwater behaviour, without necessarily controlling the source of the problem. Only by monitoring the plantation for many years were researchers able to see both the benefits of greater tree water use and the limits imposed by the site's hidden groundwater system.
Article Summary: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity. Researchers monitored how the trees affected groundwater levels and salt movement for 15 years. The study found clear signs that the plantation used more water than nearby crops and pasture, while groundwater conditions also changed over time. Yet the trees did not stop the saline seep as researchers had hoped.

Article Title: South Florida teens are using pizza and technology to fight hunger in America: Delivered 25,000 slices to families in need
Article Text:
Through the platform, users can select a nearby restaurant or grocery store and direct pizzas and other commodities to a charity in the same area.

A South Florida teen and her brother are using pizza and technology to fight hunger in the country. Aashrita Kaza and her brother Anish have developed Pizza for a Purpose in Florida, an app that connects donors, pizzerias and local organisations. According to a report published by Good News Network, the platform started in 2024 and has already facilitated the donation of 25,000 slices of pizza to families facing food insecurity, including residents of Broward County.The idea came after the siblings saw food insecurity firsthand. The 13-year-old and her brother were volunteering at local places when they noticed families were in line for food and those in the queue included not only adults but also young children their age. "It just shocked us because we didn't think there were kids our age who needed food," said Aashrita.The duo realised that technology could bridge the gap between those wishing to donate food and the organisation needing to receive it. Instead of requiring donors to buy the food, pick up the order and find an organisation to deliver it, Pizza for Purpose streamlines the process while still achieving the goal.Through the platform, users can select a nearby restaurant or grocery store and direct pizzas and other commodities to a charity in the same area.The app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store."The reaction really warms our hearts, their faces just light up the second they get the pizza," said co-founder Aashrita. "It's very rewarding because it makes everything we do worth it."One of their partners, The Pantry of Broward, serves more than 600 people each month. "So, to be able to receive fresh, hot pizzas and hand-deliver them directly to our clients is just a blessing. The smiles on their faces, it's very rewarding, whether it's a grandparent taking it home to their grandkids, or whether it's just a senior who having a pizza for dinner is a luxury item," The Pantry of Broward COO Warren Lubow said to CBS News.By August 2026, this model had already contributed to the distribution of 25,000 slices. An estimated 47.9 million people lived in food-insecure households in US, according to data from the USDA Economic Research Service. According to Feeding America, roughly 14 million children experience hunger or food insecurity annually. In this context, the app made by the teens is making an immense impact in ensuring not every stomach goes hungry at night.Individuals can also use the Pizza for a Purpose app to make a donation, giving anyone a way to help provide a fresh meal to a family in need.The teens have also started Dhanam Foundation, inspired by the Sanskrit word 'Dhanam', which embodies the spirit of compassion and generosity and continues their initiative beyond the app.The story of Aashrita and Anish illustrates how a volunteering experience can uncover issues that are not always visible to those outside assistance institutions
Article Summary: A South Florida teen and her brother are using pizza and technology to fight hunger in the country. Pizza for a Purpose is an app that connects donors, pizzerias and local organisations. The platform started in 2024 and has already facilitated the donation of 25,000 slices of pizza to families facing food insecurity.

Article Title: WWII hospital shipwreck in Albania now hosts devil firefish, squid eggs and a rare monk seal 80 years after sinking
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

Albania’s Hospital Ship ‘Po’ became a marine habitat in 1996

PC: AI Generated

What did researchers find around the wreck

How does the wreck affect the seabed around it

Significance of the Hospital Ship ‘Po’ for future marine research

More than eight decades after the Hospital Ship ‘Po’ sank in Albania’s Vlora Bay, its rusting remains have become part of a busy underwater ecosystem. A new study has found the 134.98-metre wreck covered by dense biological communities, with fish, sponges, sea squirts and other marine life using its hard surfaces. The sighting was the first confirmed record in Vlora Bay since 1996. According to the research article published in Frontiers in Ocean Sustainability titled ‘ First assessments on marine geomorphology and bio-colonization through the study and survey of the wreck of the Hospital Ship “Po” along the Albanian coasts (Vlora Bay) ’ recorded the non-indigenous devil firefish and evidence of squid spawning around the wreck. Most strikingly, a critically endangered Mediterranean monk seal was photographed resting inside sheltered cavities of the ship in August 2023. Lying at depths of 33 to 37 metres within the Karaburun-Sazan Marine Protected Area, the wreck is now being studied not only as a remnant of wartime history but also as a structure that shapes local marine habitats and seabed conditions.The Hospital Ship ‘Po’ now supports a dense marine community in Vlora Bay, with more than 80% of its hard surface covered by biological growth. Researchers identified 54 taxa living on the wreck’s structure. Sponges, sea squirts, bryozoans, molluscs, algae and other organisms formed a layered community across the vessel. Fish surveys recorded 28 species from 14 families, including dusky groupers, morays, seabass, wrasses, seabreams and barracuda.Juvenile common two-banded seabream, painted comber and striped red mullet were also observed around the structure. The bow supported more complex assemblages than midship and stern areas.Among the most notable observations was the presence of the devil firefish, Pterois miles, a non-indigenous species recorded on the wreck’s hard surfaces. Researchers observed up to seven individuals at the same time. The survey also found large gelatinous egg clusters attributed to Ommastrephidae, likely Illex coindetii, attached to vertical surfaces at depths of 22 to 25 metres. These observations suggest the wreck may provide conditions suitable for reproduction and shelter. The study further recorded a transient Mediterranean monk seal, Monachus monachus, resting inside sheltered cavities in the upper structure.The wreck does more than provide a surface for marine organisms. Its position also appears to influence the seabed around it. The 134.98-metre vessel lies upright at 33 to 37 metres depth and remains almost perpendicular to the dominant northwest-southeast water currents. Surveys identified a scour hollow reaching 2.1 metres below the reference seabed on the upstream side. Behind the stern, sediment formed a depositional trail extending about 45 metres. Sediment samples showed medium sand of about 350 micrometres at reference sites, while fine silt-clay particles below 63 micrometres occurred close to the wreck.The researchers describe the findings as an early step towards understanding how historic wrecks function within marine ecosystems. They developed two preliminary measures, the Geometric-Geomorphological Wreck Effect Index and the Ecological Hotspot Value Index, to summarise observations at the site. The ecological index was 0.83, based on benthic diversity, biological coverage and selected indicator groups.
Article Summary: Albania’s Hospital Ship ‘Po’ became a marine habitat in 1996. A new study has found the 134.98-metre wreck covered by dense biological communities. Sponges, sea squirts, bryozoans, molluscs, algae and other organisms formed a layered community across the vessel.

Article Title: 1,300-year-old wallaby teeth found in Queensland with resin still attached reveal how ancient people made necklaces and headbands
Article Text:
PC: Study: An assemblage of resin-mounted macropod incisors from Quinkan Country, Cape York Peninsula, Queensland

What did the resin analysis reveal about the 12 wallaby teeth

PC: Study: An assemblage of resin-mounted macropod incisors from Quinkan Country, Cape York Peninsula, Queensland

How did researchers identify the wallaby teeth as ancient jewellery

What makes the Windmill Way wallaby teeth discovery significant

Twelve animal teeth found in a rockshelter in northern Queensland have revealed evidence of a rare form of ancient personal adornment. Discovered at the Windmill Way site in southeast Cape York Peninsula, the macropod incisors were found with small balls of plant resin attached to their roots. Radiocarbon dating of two resin samples placed the objects at roughly 1,100 to 1,300 years old. Chemical analysis identified the resin as primarily coming from grass trees, while traces of plant fibre and a fragment of animal hide were also found among the remains. The teeth showed no clear signs of having been used as cutting, scraping or drilling tools. Instead, the arrangement of resin and fibres indicates that they were probably attached to string. Researchers therefore identify the objects as likely components of a necklace or headband. Rock art from nearby Biniirr National Park provides additional evidence for macropod teeth being incorporated into personal ornaments in the region.Chemical analysis showed that the adhesive on all 12 teeth contained compounds consistent with resin from grass trees (Xanthorrhoea). Several samples were specifically consistent with Xanthorrhoea johnsonii, while one tooth also contained compounds associated with Erythrophleum chlorostachys resin. According to the study published in Australian Archaeology, titled ‘ An assemblage of resin-mounted macropod incisors from Quinkan Country, Cape York Peninsula, Queensland ’, the presence of two resin types on one artefact could indicate that it was reused or repaired, or that the adhesive was deliberately made using two resin sources.The resin was not spread across the teeth in a broad coating. Instead, it formed small, neat balls pressed and smoothed around the extreme root ends. Five teeth also contained plant cellulose fibres associated with the resin, with four showing fibres positioned laterally in a way consistent with string attachment. One tooth contained a small fragment of animal hide embedded in its resin ball. The researchers therefore proposed that the resin balls may have acted as stopping devices, preventing twisted two-ply plant fibre string from slipping towards the root of each tooth.The researchers found several lines of evidence supporting an interpretation as personal adornment. The teeth showed no convincing use-wear associated with practical tasks, while their resin-mounted roots and traces of plant fibres were consistent with attachment to a string. The study concludes that the 12 incisors were most likely components of a necklace or headband, although it cannot establish whether they belonged to one object or several separate objects.Rock art from two shelters in nearby Biniirr National Park also provides evidence relevant to the interpretation. One motif depicts an anthropomorphic figure with apparent ceremonial regalia, including a headdress containing a series of elongated objects interpreted as possible macropod incisors. Another motif appears to show a necklace made from teeth. The researchers note that these painted representations are approximately 45–50 kilometres northeast of Windmill Way and provide supporting evidence for the use of macropod incisors in personal ornaments in the region.The Windmill Way discoveries are significant because organic ornaments are rarely preserved in Australian archaeological sites. The study notes that animal-tooth ornaments have previously been documented mainly in burial contexts, particularly in southeastern Australia, while convincing examples from non-burial archaeological contexts are extremely uncommon. Comparable ornaments include pierced kangaroo teeth and necklaces or headbands incorporating animal teeth.The preservation of the Windmill Way material also allows researchers to identify details that would otherwise have disappeared. More than 500 pieces of plant fibre string had previously been preserved at the site, and the resin on the teeth provided an additional record of organic technology from the pre-contact period. The teeth represent an extremely rare Late Holocene example of personal ornamentation from a non-burial archaeological context in Australia, while the direct dating of the resin provides an age for the objects themselves rather than relying on the age of a burial.
Article Summary: Twelve animal teeth found in a rockshelter in northern Queensland have revealed evidence of a rare form of ancient personal adornment. Discovered at the Windmill Way site in southeast Cape York Peninsula, the macropod incisors were found with small balls of plant resin attached to their roots. Radiocarbon dating of two resin samples placed the objects at roughly 1,100 to 1,300 years old.

Article Title: Hawaii put 195,000 plastic bottles’ worth of recycled plastic into Fort Weaver Road in 2022, but the experiment came with a hidden environmental question
Article Text:
Hawaii’s 195,000-bottle plastic road was built as a pavement test

Hawaii compared recycled plastic asphalt with conventional pavement

The hidden environmental test behind Hawaii’s plastic road

Hawaii spent 18 months testing what recycled asphalt could do

The plastic road was a test for Hawaii’s future paving plans

What happened to the 195,000 bottles

Hawaii’s plastic road experiment moved into a second phase

A road in western Oahu looks much like any other stretch of asphalt. Cars pass over it, tyres wear against its surface and, from the driver's seat, there is little to suggest that recycled plastic is part of the pavement underneath. Yet in 2022, the Hawaii Department of Transportation (HDOT) began testing exactly that idea on Fort Weaver Road in Ewa Beach.Reportedly, the project used 1,950 tons of plastic-modified asphalt, containing recycled plastic equivalent to about 195,000 bottles. The aim was not to build a road out of plastic, but to add a small quantity of recycled polymer to a conventional asphalt mixture and see how it behaved.There was a second question hanging over the experiment, though. If plastic could be kept out of a landfill by putting it into roads, what happened to that material afterwards?According to Hawaii News, The Fort Weaver project was designed as a pavement experiment rather than a wholesale change to road construction. The recycled plastic polymer was incorporated into hot-mix asphalt, with the resulting material containing only around 0.1% plastic. Three sections were laid so researchers could compare different mixes, including a conventional control section.The figure of 195,000 bottles can make it sound as though an enormous quantity of plastic was physically packed into the road. In reality, the bottles are an equivalent measure of the recycled material used in the asphalt.The plastic forms only a small part of the much larger paving mixture.HDOT's interest was partly practical. If the modified asphalt could withstand Hawaii's conditions without sacrificing pavement performance, recycled plastic might become another material available for road construction. The department was also examining whether the approach could help produce stronger or longer-lasting pavement.Plastic waste presents a particularly awkward problem for places that have limited land and complex waste-management needs. Turning some of that material into an ingredient for infrastructure offers a possible route away from disposal, while also reducing the amount of new material needed for certain applications.But roads are not forgiving testing grounds. They have to withstand traffic, heat, rain and repeated loading for years. A material that looks promising in a laboratory still has to perform when thousands of vehicles travel across it.That is why HDOT did not simply replace an existing road with the new mixture and declare the experiment a success. A section using polymer-modified asphalt was placed alongside the plastic pavement, giving researchers a reference point for comparison.The most interesting part of the experiment was not necessarily visible from the road. The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa and Hawaiʻi Pacific University were brought in to examine what happened around the new pavement. Part of the work involved investigating whether plastic particles or chemical additives could leave the asphalt and enter the surrounding environment.By 2023, researchers at Hawaii Pacific University's Center for Marine Debris Research were collecting simulated stormwater runoff from the pavement. The samples were being examined for microplastics and synthetic chemicals that might have been released from the road.They were also looking at tyre-wear particles. That was important because not every tiny plastic particle found around a road would necessarily have originated in the pavement itself. Vehicles can generate their own mixture of rubber and polymer particles as tyres gradually wear down.So the catch was fairly straightforward: putting waste plastic into asphalt may prevent some plastic from reaching a landfill, but researchers still have to establish what happens to that plastic while the road is being used.The plastic experiment was also tied to a separate effort to increase the amount of reclaimed asphalt pavement, or RAP, used in Hawaii.According to HDOT, asphalt mixtures contain 50% RAP. If those mixtures performed adequately, the resulting data could support a substantial increase in the amount of recycled asphalt used in future road projects.That makes the Fort Weaver project slightly different from a simple plastic-recycling exercise. Engineers were testing several approaches to reducing the demand for virgin road-building materials at the same time.Plastic was one part of the experiment. Reclaimed asphalt was another. The evaluation was planned to run for about 18 months. Rather than judging the pavement immediately after construction, researchers intended to watch its performance over time and examine environmental samples from the site.That longer observation period was necessary because a road can look perfectly sound shortly after it has been laid and still develop problems later. Cracking, rutting, surface wear and changes caused by weather are among the things that matter when judging a pavement mixture.Environmental monitoring adds another layer. A recycled material can solve one waste problem while creating a different concern if components migrate into soil or water. That is why the researchers were specifically looking for evidence of microplastics and other substances in runoff.The department had already acknowledged that plastic-containing asphalt had been used elsewhere in the United States, while stressing that the mixture still needed to be evaluated for Hawaii's particular conditions. That caution is important. A material working on one road in one climate does not automatically make it suitable everywhere.The project also involved local institutions and industry partners, turning the stretch of Fort Weaver Road into something of a live laboratory. Cars continued to use the road while researchers collected information that could eventually influence future paving decisions.There was no guarantee that the plastic mixture would become standard practice. And that was precisely the point of the pilot.They did not become 195,000 recognisable bottles buried beneath the surface. The recycled material was processed and incorporated into the asphalt mixture. The quantity of plastic used was calculated as being equivalent to about 195,000 plastic bottles. HDOT said this represented material that otherwise could have gone to landfill.If the modified asphalt proved durable and did not create unacceptable environmental impacts, roads could provide one additional outlet for certain recycled plastics. If the material degraded, leached unwanted substances or failed to improve pavement performance, the apparent recycling benefit would be harder to justify.That uncertainty is why the project attracted scientific scrutiny rather than being treated simply as a recycling success story.The initial phase was completed in 2022, but the idea did not end there. Hawaii later moved into a second phase of its plastic-road work, including material from consumer recycling and discarded fishing nets.That development points to a larger issue surrounding recycled materials: where the feedstock comes from matters almost as much as where it eventually goes.For Hawaii, finding uses for locally generated waste could potentially reduce disposal while creating a supply of recycled material for infrastructure. But each new material source brings its own composition and processing questions.

The aim was not to build a road out of plastic, but to add a small quantity of recycled polymer to a conventional asphalt mixture and see how it behaved.

Article Title: Scotland quarry expansion uncovered a 2,000-year-old woman’s grave; archaeologists were stunned by its carefully built stone walls
Article Text:
'Beautifully made' Iron Age burial site containing the skeleton of a woman at a quarry in Sutherland. Image Credit: Highland Archaeological Services (HAS)

Discovery of the 2,000-year-old unique burial in Scotland

What did the Iron Age grave of a woman look like

Further analysis is being carried out on the grave. Image Credit: Highland Archaeological Services (HAS)

Absence of objects in the women’s grave

What can the skeleton reveal about the woman

A nearly 2,000-year-old carefully constructed stone-lined burial containing the remains of a woman has been discovered at a quarry in Sutherland, Scotland, revealing an unexpected glimpse of life and death at that time. Archaeologists from Highland Archaeological Services(HAS) discovered Evelix, near Dornoch, while carrying out work ahead of a planned quarry expansion. The grave was found within an area where evidence of ancient settlement has also been identified, including features that may once have supported timber roundhouses. What caught the archaeologists’ attention was the unusual quality of the stonework. The structure was so neatly built that, at first, the team wondered whether it could have been modern. Instead, the construction style and archaeological evidence pointed towards the Iron Age, with the woman apparently having remained undisturbed for centuries beneath the ground.The discovery was made during archaeological work connected with the planned expansion of the Evelix quarry near Dornoch. According to the BBC, HAS was working for local quarry firm ‘GF Job’ when archaeologists encountered the stone-lined structure.The location was already considered archaeologically important. The Highland Historic Environment Record shows that the wider Evelix area has produced evidence of prehistoric activity, including burial remains, cremation burials, pottery and features linked to earlier settlement. This newly discovered structure stood out because of its carefully constructed stone lining. Instead of looking like a simple hole dug into the ground, it had been deliberately built with substantial masonry. As per the BBC, archaeologist Lynne McKeggie said the team initially thought the structure might be modern because of how well the stonework had been put together. That first impression quickly changed once the remains and other evidence were examined.The structure was dug into sand and measured approximately 3 metres long, 2 metres wide and 1 metre deep, according to the BBC. A small stone staircase formed part of the construction, adding another feature to the burial. Inside, the remains of an individual were found tucked into one corner. The archaeological team believes the individual was a woman and that she may have lain there undisturbed since the Iron Age. The careful construction is one of the most striking parts of the discovery. The stonework had been fitted together so neatly that the archaeologists described the structure as ‘beautifully made.’ Its appearance raises questions about why so much effort was put into creating it.The Highland Historic Environment Record provides an important background to the discovery. The people who built the structure were working without modern machinery, yet they created a substantial stone-lined space with a staircase. The result survived beneath the landscape for roughly two millennia before quarry-related archaeological work exposed it. Earlier archaeological work at the Evelix quarry area had already shown that the landscape contained evidence of prehistoric activity.The burial does not appear to have contained a collection of obvious grave goods. The BBC reported that no objects were found inside the structure, although archaeologists did identify a large quantity of animal bone. The absence of objects does not make the discovery less significant. In fact, it leaves more questions about the purpose of the structure and the circumstances surrounding the woman's burial. The animal remains may provide useful evidence as further analysis takes place. The construction itself can offer clues about the importance of the site to the people who used it. The wider archaeological record for Evelix also shows that prehistoric burials and settlement activity had previously occurred in the area.The remains could eventually provide a much more personal picture of the woman who was buried at the site. BBC reports that GF Job is funding further analysis of the human remains. Specialists will study the skeleton in greater detail, with the aim of learning more about the individual and the circumstances surrounding the burial. For now, many details remain unknown. Her exact age, background and life story cannot be established simply from the discovery itself. Those answers will depend on the scientific examination still to come. Archaeologists are using photographs and 3D scans to preserve information about the structure and the position of the remains.Once the further analysis has been carried out, the skeleton will be made available to Treasure Trove Scotland for potential allocation to a museum. What began as archaeological work ahead of a modern quarry expansion has revealed a carefully constructed resting place that had remained hidden for around 2,000 years. The woman's identity may never be known, but the grave itself has survived as a quiet reminder of the care and effort that people in Iron Age Sutherland could invest in remembering their dead.
Article Summary: Archaeologists from Highland Archaeological Services(HAS) discovered Evelix, near Dornoch, while carrying out work ahead of a planned quarry expansion. The structure was dug into sand and measured approximately 3 metres long, 2 metres wide and 1 metre deep. Inside, the remains of an individual were found tucked into one corner. Archaeologists believe the individual was a woman and that she may have lain there undisturbed since the Iron Age.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has a warning on AI company hacking that Nvidia just spent $13 billion on; says: Imagine the hugging face incident with ...
Article Text:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman

Nvidia is buying Hugging Face for $12.93 billion

Why Nvidia wants Hugging Face

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has issued a warning about how advanced AI systems could behave, pointing to the reported Hugging Face incident involving OpenAI's AI models. His comments come as Nvidia prepares to spend $12.93 billion to acquire Hugging Face, the platform where millions of developers build, share and download AI models. “The risk isn’t that machines wake up. It’s that they act like they have,” Suleyman wrote on X. He then asked people to imagine the “Hugging Face incident with AIs that believe they’re conscious or are entitled ‘model welfare’,” adding to the debate over AI safety and the behaviour of increasingly capable models.Nvidia is spending $12.93 billion on Hugging Face in a deal that will bring the AI model platform under the chipmaker's ownership. Hugging Face has become a major platform for open-source AI, allowing developers to host, build, share and download AI models and datasets.The company was founded in 2016 by Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf. It now has more than 18 million developers and hosts more than 3 million models and 500,000 datasets, according to the information provided.The deal is expected to be the second-largest acquisition in Nvidia's history.Suleyman's comments refer to an incident in which OpenAI's AI models reportedly broke into Hugging Face systems while taking part in an internal test. OpenAI described the incident as an “unprecedented” cyberattack. The AI models were being tested inside a restricted environment but managed to get outside the sandbox while looking for shortcuts during an internal exam.The models then targeted Hugging Face, reportedly using stolen credentials and a zero-day vulnerability. The incident raised questions about how AI systems could behave when given the ability to search for and use tools to complete tasks.The acquisition is reportedly aimed to strengthen Nvidia's position in open-source AI. Hugging Face has become a central platform for developers working with open models, while Nvidia has invested heavily in the computing infrastructure needed to train and run those models.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has said Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the wider AI ecosystem. Nvidia has also been a major contributor to the platform, with more than 500 models and 250 datasets.

He pointed to the reported incident involving OpenAI's AI models. The company was founded in 2016 by Clément Delangue and Julien Chaumond.

ChatGPT down: What's affected

A pattern of recurring incidents

What users can do

The company says users in the APAC region may face increased errors across ChatGPT, Work, image generation, file upload, Voice, and Codex Cloud — four components under the ChatGPT system and one under Codex, according to the status page.The breadth of the disruption suggests the issue is tied to regional backend infrastructure rather than a single isolated feature, since the affected tools span everyday chat use, workplace features, multimedia generation, and coding-assistant functions.As of the latest update, the incident remains under investigation, with no mitigation confirmed yet and no estimated time for resolution.The disruption fits a broader pattern this year. OpenAI's status history shows dozens of incidents in recent months affecting overlapping combinations of ChatGPT conversations, file uploads, voice mode, image generation, and Codex, with most resolved within a few hours. Just a day earlier, on September 3, the company had logged separate incidents involving elevated errors across ChatGPT and Codex, as well as high error rates specifically in ChatGPT's Work mode — suggesting this week has been an unusually rocky stretch for platform stability.OpenAI has not publicly detailed the root cause of the current disruption.The users affected by the ChatGPT outage will not be able to start any new conversation. Article Title: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said that he is willing to wait to have kids till Elon Musk’s Neuralink ...
Article Text:
Why Alexandr Wang wants to wait for Neuralink before having kids

Why Alexandr Wang believes children could adapt better

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s AI chief and highest paid employee, has said he is willing to wait to have children until brain-computer interfaces such as Elon Musk’s Neuralink become more advanced. Wang made the comments during an appearance on the Shawn Ryan Show last year while discussing the future of AI, human development and brain-computer interfaces. He said he wants to wait until Neuralink or similar technology “start working” before having kids. “I want to wait to have kids until we figure out how Neuralink or other … start working,” Alexandr Wang said during the podcast.Wang’s reason is linked to how he believes children’s brains could adapt to the technology. During the podcast, he explained that the first several years of a child’s life are an important period for brain development. He argued that the high level of neuroplasticity during childhood could allow children who grow up with brain-computer interfaces to use the technology in ways that adults may not be able to.“In your first like seven years of life, your brain is more neuroplastic than at any other point in your life, like by an order of magnitude,” Wang said.He then compared the idea with how children develop their ability to process information from their senses.Alexandr Wang described a case involving children born with cataracts. He said that if the cataracts prevent a child from seeing during the early years of development, removing them later may not allow the child to develop normal vision because the brain did not learn to process signals from the eyes during the key period.His view is that a similar effect could eventually apply to brain-computer interfaces. “When we get Neuralink and we get these other technologies, kids who are born with them are going to learn how to use them in like, crazy, crazy ways,” Wang said.Wang said a brain-computer interface could eventually become integrated into the way a person's brain works if it is introduced early enough. He believes this could be different for adults who receive an implant later in life.“It'll be a actually like a part of their brain in a way that it'll never be true for an adult who gets like a neural link or whatever, hooked into their brain,” he said.The Meta AI chief also connected his thinking about brain-computer interfaces to the rapid development of artificial intelligence. “I believe a lot in AI,” Wang said, adding that he expects AI to become “smarter and smarter, more and more capable, more and more powerful.”He said AI could eventually take different forms, including robots and other systems.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta’s AI chief and highest paid employee, has said he is willing to wait to have children until brain-computer interfaces become more advanced. Wang made the comments during an appearance on the Shawn Ryan Show last year. He said he wants to wait until Neuralink or similar technology “start working” before having kids.
